content: In certain species of diatoms, auxospores are specialized cells that are produced during critical stages of their cell cycle or life history. These cells are primarily involved in processes such as growth, sexual reproduction, or dormancy. Auxospores play a crucial role in restoring the normal size of diatom cells, as repeated mitotic cell divisions result in a progressive reduction in cell size. This size reduction occurs because, during each division, the daughter cells inherit one of the two silica valves that make up the cell wall and subsequently form a smaller valve within the inherited one. As a result, the average size of diatom cells in a population decreases with each division cycle. When a diatom cell becomes too small, it produces an auxospore to restore its size to the normal dimensions characteristic of vegetative cells. Auxospores are also involved in the sexual reproduction of diatoms. They may form after the fusion of haploid gametes, resulting in the creation of a diploid zygote. Additionally, auxospores can serve as dormant stages, often referred to as resting spores. These dormant forms enable diatoms to survive during unfavorable environmental conditions, such as nutrient depletion or the winter season.
